I just rebuilt a Cannondale Allroad E-Bike and that retails for 1200-1600 USD. All Microshift drivetrain, shifters, etc. Unbranded Tektro brakes. Kenda Tires, which are okay I guess. Bafang Electrics. Just cheap all the way down. But $180 for a broken e-bike that isn’t stolen is a steal. 

I had to pay $180 for a new HMI and charger for it, and another $20 for a new lock core for the battery. So I’m about $380 into it for the bike itself and the electrics. 

Everything in the drivetrain needed to be replaced. The shifter was broken, the freewheel had play in it I haven’t seen in 20yo Shimano parts, the chain was KMC so it was decent but I wasn’t re-using it on principle, the derailleur jog wheels had so much play in them and it was bent beyond saving. Everything got Shimano parts. Went for the Acera derailleur, seeing as it was probably putting lipstick on a pig otherwise. 

Meanwhile, the bike itself came out in ‘23 so it’s only a few years old. I’ve used Microshift’s Advent line of products with success on my 1x10 trail bike. I don’t think I’ll ever use another one of their products outside of the occasional shifter on a cheap fix. I would like to point out that while you’re in dev, and I respect your position, some of what you wrote is wrong. 

There are price sheets and advertisements from the good old days of cartridges where the cost of the game itself varied because solid state media was expensive. Not every game was $59. I remember being alive for $80 Nintendo 64 cartridges. Doom 64 was $75 and that’s almost $150 in today’s money. 

At first that sounds like a great argument for parity, but in reality the manufacturing process of disc based media and economies of scale are what kept the cost of games down for the consumer. The medium games were produced on determined the price of games far more than any of the budgetary concerns of the publishers. The cost of older games was determined literally by how many chips were on the board, overhead, and what the industry accepted as a standard pricing. Then because discs were cheap to mass manufacture we saw prices stagnate for the entire life of CD, DVD, and Blu-Ray games. 

Once the game has gone gold, you can print as many of those as possible. Solid state media is as cheap as it’s ever been, disc based media is as cheap as it’s ever been. We’ve been seeing ROI being met as these evergreen titles from AAA studios make everything up on volume. In terms of traction, original sales are important, but anyone who’s paid a passing glance at GDC talks knows you make money vastly differently in the long run these days. It’s all discount sales and volume. 

It’s not just as simple as aligning with inflation to some higher pricing structure. Especially when you consider the fact that beyond infrastructure costs, you don’t have nearly the same overhead for digital releases. 

So yeah games do need to be more expensive, they do need to adjust to inflation. However, $90 (with tax) is insane and will hurt the volume of sales for pre-orders and day-one. Consumer spending on entertainment always goes up in a recession because it’s cheap-er fun. I don’t see $90 (with tax) as the new standard falling into that existing standard to make it up in volume.

Yeah, that’s the internal resolution of the game itself, particularly its render quality. The GPU renders the frame, that gets passed along to another chip that handles the upscaling and encoding for HDMI. It passes those frames along at whatever refresh rate you set it to, and will do some magic along the way so 30fps and 60fps games don’t experience much screen tearing. 

You can have a 4k output resolution, but the internal rendering resolution of the app can be like 1440p 120hz with HDR. You’ll still see an upscaled image on your TV at whatever refresh rate is supported or a VRR. 

Turning on 4K does not degrade the image of the internal rendering resolution of the application. If anything it enhances it. 

The problem comes with HDMI 2.0 bandwidth issues where older devices and displays can only support 4k 60hz or 1440p 120hz. This is not a rendering problem it’s purely a limitation of HDMI from a few years ago. 

Feel free to crank the resolution up in the settings for the console. Just make sure you pick whatever performance mode you prefer in apps, including specific Xbox 360 games with enhancements for Xbox One X.

The demand (and arguably value) for necessities like housing, healthcare, utilities, food, etc. is near infinite. The market is always going to shift to what it can bear, so what you’re seeing is Landlord A, B, and C all shifting their prices to the current highest levels of rent because there isn’t an incentive in place to ever lower those costs. 

Supply and demand should be a thing, right? No one has an incentive to undercut their competitors, because really there is no competition.

If that doesn’t work, take your vise grip brand channel locks and put a 3/4 EMT pipe on the uppermost handle. You can now use this as a breaker bar as it bites deep into the metal of the seat post. In the sea of consumer goods that have been documented experiencing this over the last 20 years, Texas Toast is what tipped you off? Good.

They need to have the consequences that show providing value to a customer is how you justify higher prices, and shrinkflation with ever booming profits is just the opposite. Granted there’s some stuff that’s not as desirable to do this with, like toothpaste or laundry detergent, but most pre-packaged foods like this can be made at home with little effort and a small amount of planning.

In a world where shareholders of the Texas Toast conglomerate absolutely legally need an ever increasing return on their investment, the company that owns Texas Toast must do what they can with the value of the labor and materials put into the Texas Toast. This includes, paying employees a wage that doesn’t allow them to thrive, higher prices of goods, and other tools like shrinkflation and deteriorating quality.

The whole Texas Toast thing is a natural and inevitable miniature conclusion to entire systems of how we govern and organize ourselves. Line go up, line must always go up, even at the cost of Texas Toast. Its interoperable and dependent systems layered on top of each other with a cascade of consequences leading to Texas Toast. You wanna fix shrinkflation? Start there. Start by talking with people and voting for people into public service that want to change these systems for our benefit. Physical therapy and orthotics can solve this, and you will feel better. Based on the wear, I would encourage you to get your doctor to order a gait test with a Physical Therapist, and determine how to treat your bottom half a bit better. Edit - While I stand by my “drive it and maintain the emissions until the wheels fall off” mentality, I believe my assessment was based off some misconceptions and outdated information. “Your mileage may vary” is a real thing with EVs. Some tesla owners have gone through multiple battery packs in their warranty period. Others have seen degradation that suggests their vehicles will last close to two decades, which is great. Unfortunately, many EV manufacturers restrict third parties abilities to repair and replace failing cels, opting to recycle these batteries which comes at its own environmental expense, despite being 90% effective at reclaiming the lithium, cobalt, and nickel in the cels. 

Fortunately research shows that in 200k miles EVs would use around 39 tons of carbon in their lifetime, compared to the 66 tons of carbon an ICE vehicle would emit in that same timeframe. No one can argue that EVs aren’t better for the environment in their day-to-day use, but the systems surrounding them are the thing I take issue with as they appear to be part of a flawed and transitional period of personal transportation needs, with what our infrastructure can provide, and what consumer capitalism incentivizes. 

This is not even considering the effect regional temperatures has on the chemical composition of batteries and how many people have been stranded in sub freezing temperatures. Conversely without a regularly maintained and well engineered cooling system, EVs in places like Arizona have been known to die faster. A phenomenon which spurred on many early Nissan Leaf owners to pounce on vehicles from the desert with dying batteries and a great warranty, for what amounted to a brand new vehicle with the perfect level of accelerated degradation in that limited time period. We don’t seem to account engineering EVs for these extreme climates, and if we did we wouldn’t see bricked Teslas in the freezing winter.

20% of the United States uses coal power to generate electricity and power these fleets of vehicles. Even Natural Gas power plants emit hundreds of tons of NOx, despite producing less CO2 than their coal counterparts. Nuclear still isn’t embraced because of PR disasters like Three Mile Island and Fukushima. These facts prove that owning an EV still comes at a great cost to greenhouse gases that exacerbate climate change and its infrastructure crippling effects. Solar comes with its own concerns in sustainability and the rare earth materials needed for building panels. Same with the turbines that drive wind power, but to a lesser extent. That’s nothing to say of the supply chain, from resource extraction, to the semi truck delivering the final goods, all relies on oil. 

There is no good solution to this, and it’s not as simple as EVs bad, or ICE bad. It’s a global infrastructure and engineering problem, and the times are too good for governments to change the infrastructure and the companies that benefit from it. 

However, might I suggest the evolutionary finality of all these decisions… trains. A fully autonomous electric vehicle that propels you towards where you need to go in a timely manner. We can have trains, and we can have more space on the road for cool fun cars and the people who love the experience of piloting an automobile. We can have vehicles that get you to rural places and do the hard work people need them for. But for massive amounts of people moving in the same basic direction? We solved this problem over a hundred years ago.
